intro.title: An online shop's orders
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Welcome to the capstone quest. Each one is a full piece of work on a database of its own, using skills from across the course: you'll choose which tables to join, how to group, when a window or a CTE is the right tool, and which NULLs to watch out for. The challenges say what the result should look like, not how to get it, so there is usually more than one good answer.

The first is a small online shop selling tea, coffee and kitchen things. The owner wants a report on the last six months: what sold, who bought it, how the months compare and how much the discounts cost.

The tables are `customers`, `products`, `orders` (with a `status`: only `paid` orders count as sales) and `order_items`, one row for each product in an order, with the `quantity` and the `unit_price` actually charged. That can be lower than the product's list `price` when there was a discount, so revenue is always `quantity * unit_price`.

A good habit for a report like this: start from the smallest correct query, check its rows by eye, then build on it. Here, most answers start from paid orders joined to their items:

```
SELECT o.id AS order_id, o.ordered_on, c.name AS customer,
       ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY o.id, o.ordered_on, c.name
ORDER BY o.ordered_on, o.id;
```

challenges.title: Easy: Sales so far
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show one row: the number of paid orders (`paid_orders`) and their `revenue` (2 decimals).
challenges.hint: Join orders to order_items, keep `status = 'paid'`, and count the orders with `COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)`: each order has several item rows.
challenges.solution:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS paid_orders,
       ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';

challenges.title: Easy: Order totals
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each paid order, show `order_id`, `ordered_on`, the customer's name (`customer`) and the order's `total` (2 decimals). In date order, then by order id.
challenges.hint: The intro's example.

SELECT o.id AS order_id, o.ordered_on, c.name AS customer,
       ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY o.id, o.ordered_on, c.name
ORDER BY o.ordered_on, o.id;

challenges.title: Easy: Signed up, never ordered
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `name` and `email` of customers who have never placed an order of any kind. Sort by name.
challenges.hint: `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT name, email
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
ORDER BY name;

challenges.title: Medium: Month by month
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each month with paid orders (`month`, like `2026-05`), show the number of paid `orders` and the `revenue` (2 decimals). In month order.
challenges.hint: `strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered_on) AS month`, grouped by it.
challenges.solution:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered_on) AS month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

challenges.title: Medium: Best seller in each category
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each `category`, show its best-selling product by units in paid orders (`product`, and `units`). Keep ties. Sort by category, then product.
challenges.hint: Units per product in a CTE with `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY SUM(i.quantity) DESC)`, then keep rank 1.
challenges.solution:
WITH units AS (
  SELECT p.category, p.name AS product, SUM(i.quantity) AS units,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY SUM(i.quantity) DESC) AS place
  FROM order_items i
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = i.order_id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY p.id, p.category, p.name
)
SELECT category, product, units
FROM units
WHERE place = 1
ORDER BY category, product;

challenges.title: Medium: Average basket
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each customer with paid orders, show `name`, their number of paid `orders` and their average order value (`average_order`, 2 decimals). Highest average first, then by name.
challenges.hint: Revenue divided by `COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT o.id), 2) AS average_order
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY average_order DESC, c.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Up or down
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each month with paid orders, show `month`, `revenue` (2 decimals) and the change from the month before as a percentage (`change_pct`, 1 decimal; empty for the first month). In month order.
challenges.hint: Monthly revenue in a CTE, then `100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered_on) AS month, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY month
)
SELECT month, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS change_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

challenges.title: Hard: Coming back
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the customers with two or more paid orders: `name`, `orders`, their first and last paid order dates (`first_order`, `last_order`) and the whole days between them (`days_between`). Most orders first, then by name.
challenges.hint: Group paid orders by customer with `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2`; `CAST(julianday(MAX(…)) - julianday(MIN(…)) AS INTEGER)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS orders,
       MIN(o.ordered_on) AS first_order, MAX(o.ordered_on) AS last_order,
       CAST(julianday(MAX(o.ordered_on)) - julianday(MIN(o.ordered_on)) AS INTEGER) AS days_between
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY orders DESC, c.name;

challenges.title: Expert: What the discounts cost
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each product sold below its list price in paid orders, show the product's name (`product`), the units sold at a discount (`discounted_units`) and the money given away (`given_away`: list price minus price charged, times quantity; 2 decimals). Most given away first, then by product.
challenges.hint: Join items to products and orders; `WHERE i.unit_price < p.price AND o.status = 'paid'`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT p.name AS product, SUM(i.quantity) AS discounted_units,
       ROUND(SUM((p.price - i.unit_price) * i.quantity), 2) AS given_away
FROM order_items i
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
JOIN orders o ON o.id = i.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'paid' AND i.unit_price < p.price
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY given_away DESC, product;

challenges.title: Expert: Customer summary
challenges.promptMarkdown: Create a view `customer_summary` with every customer's `name`, `city`, paid `orders` (0 if none), `revenue` (2 decimals, 0 if none), date of their last paid order (`last_order`, empty if none) and `place` (RANK by revenue, highest first).
challenges.hint: Inside the view: a CTE of paid totals per customer, LEFT JOINed to customers, with COALESCE and `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY …)`.
challenges.solution:
CREATE VIEW customer_summary AS
WITH paid AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders,
         SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue, MAX(o.ordered_on) AS last_order
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, c.city,
       COALESCE(p.orders, 0) AS orders,
       ROUND(COALESCE(p.revenue, 0), 2) AS revenue,
       p.last_order,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COALESCE(p.revenue, 0) DESC) AS place
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN paid p ON p.customer_id = c.id;

questions.prompt: Ben's only order is unpaid. Which query keeps Ben, with a NULL total?

choices.label: `customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'`
`customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'paid'`
`customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'`
`customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'paid'`

questions.explanation: A test in ON only decides which orders match, so the LEFT JOIN keeps Ben with NULLs. The same test in WHERE runs after the join and removes him, because NULL = 'paid' is not true.

questions.prompt: Revenue is 100 in June and 120 in July. What does `ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1)` give for July?
questions.explanation: LAG gives the previous month, 100. (120 − 100) / 100 is 0.2, which is 20.0 per cent. For June there is no earlier month, so it gives NULL.

intro.title: A school's grades
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A school wants its term's marks worked out. Students are enrolled on `courses`; each course has `assessments`, each with a `weight` (a course's weights add up to 100) and a due date; `results` holds each student's `score` out of 100.

One rule matters more than any other here: **work that wasn't handed in has no row in results**, and it counts as 0. A plain join from results would quietly skip it and make the student look better. So start from what should exist, every enrolled student with every assessment of their course, and LEFT JOIN the results onto that:

```
SELECT c.title AS course, s.name,
       ROUND(SUM(COALESCE(r.score, 0) * a.weight) / 100.0, 1) AS mark
FROM enrolments e
JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id
JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
JOIN assessments a ON a.course_id = e.course_id
LEFT JOIN results r ON r.assessment_id = a.id AND r.student_id = e.student_id
GROUP BY e.student_id, e.course_id, c.title, s.name
ORDER BY course, mark DESC, s.name;
```

The course mark is the weighted sum: each score times its weight, added up, divided by 100. Multiplying whole numbers first and dividing by `100.0` at the end keeps it exact, so two students on the same marks really do tie.

Grades are bands of the mark: A from 80, B from 65, C from 50, F below that.

challenges.title: Medium: Letter grades
challenges.promptMarkdown: The same, with a `grade` beside each mark: `A` from 80, `B` from 65, `C` from 50, `F` below. Columns `course`, `name`, `mark`, `grade`. Sort by course, then highest mark, then name.
challenges.hint: Work the marks out in a CTE, then a CASE on the mark.
challenges.solution:
WITH marks AS (
  SELECT c.title AS course, s.name, e.student_id,
         SUM(COALESCE(r.score, 0) * a.weight) / 100.0 AS mark
  FROM enrolments e
  JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id
  JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
  JOIN assessments a ON a.course_id = e.course_id
  LEFT JOIN results r ON r.assessment_id = a.id AND r.student_id = e.student_id
  GROUP BY e.student_id, e.course_id, c.title, s.name
)
SELECT course, name, ROUND(mark, 1) AS mark,
       CASE WHEN mark >= 80 THEN 'A' WHEN mark >= 65 THEN 'B' WHEN mark >= 50 THEN 'C' ELSE 'F' END AS grade
FROM marks
ORDER BY course, mark DESC, name;

challenges.title: Hard: Class rank
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each student's `place` on each course (RANK by mark, highest first; equal marks share a place): `course`, `name`, `mark` (1 decimal), `place`. Sort by course, then place, then name.
challenges.hint: `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY course ORDER BY mark DESC)` on the marks CTE.
challenges.solution:
WITH marks AS (
  SELECT c.title AS course, s.name, e.student_id,
         SUM(COALESCE(r.score, 0) * a.weight) / 100.0 AS mark
  FROM enrolments e
  JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id
  JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
  JOIN assessments a ON a.course_id = e.course_id
  LEFT JOIN results r ON r.assessment_id = a.id AND r.student_id = e.student_id
  GROUP BY e.student_id, e.course_id, c.title, s.name
)
SELECT course, name, ROUND(mark, 1) AS mark,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY course ORDER BY mark DESC) AS place
FROM marks
ORDER BY course, place, name;

challenges.title: Hard: Grade table
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each course with students, show `course` and how many students got each grade, as columns `a`, `b`, `c` and `f`. Sort by course.
challenges.hint: Marks in a CTE, then `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE mark >= 80) AS a` and so on.
challenges.solution:
WITH marks AS (
  SELECT c.title AS course, s.name, e.student_id,
         SUM(COALESCE(r.score, 0) * a.weight) / 100.0 AS mark
  FROM enrolments e
  JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id
  JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
  JOIN assessments a ON a.course_id = e.course_id
  LEFT JOIN results r ON r.assessment_id = a.id AND r.student_id = e.student_id
  GROUP BY e.student_id, e.course_id, c.title, s.name
)
SELECT course,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE mark >= 80) AS a,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE mark >= 65 AND mark < 80) AS b,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE mark >= 50 AND mark < 65) AS c,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE mark < 50) AS f
FROM marks
GROUP BY course
ORDER BY course;

challenges.title: Expert: Progress
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each student and course with at least two results, show `name`, `course`, the score of their earliest handed-in assessment (`first_score`), of their latest (`last_score`) and the `change`. Biggest rise first, then by name, then course.
challenges.hint: Number each student's results on a course both ways by due date (ROW_NUMBER), count them with `COUNT(*) OVER (…)`, then pick the first and last with `MAX(CASE WHEN … THEN score END)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT s.name, c.title AS course, res.score,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY res.student_id, a.course_id ORDER BY a.due_on) AS first_no,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY res.student_id, a.course_id ORDER BY a.due_on DESC) AS last_no,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY res.student_id, a.course_id) AS handed_in
  FROM results res
  JOIN assessments a ON a.id = res.assessment_id
  JOIN students s ON s.id = res.student_id
  JOIN courses c ON c.id = a.course_id
)
SELECT name, course,
       MAX(CASE WHEN first_no = 1 THEN score END) AS first_score,
       MAX(CASE WHEN last_no = 1 THEN score END) AS last_score,
       MAX(CASE WHEN last_no = 1 THEN score END) - MAX(CASE WHEN first_no = 1 THEN score END) AS change
FROM r
WHERE handed_in >= 2
GROUP BY name, course
ORDER BY change DESC, name, course;

challenges.title: Expert: Report cards
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show one row per student with courses: `name`, number of `courses`, their `average` course mark (1 decimal), and their best course (`best_course`: highest mark, the first title alphabetically on a tie). Highest average first, then by name.
challenges.hint: Marks CTE, then ROW_NUMBER per student by mark DESC, course; group by student and pick the best with `MAX(CASE WHEN n = 1 THEN course END)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH marks AS (
  SELECT c.title AS course, s.name, e.student_id,
         SUM(COALESCE(r.score, 0) * a.weight) / 100.0 AS mark
  FROM enrolments e
  JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id
  JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
  JOIN assessments a ON a.course_id = e.course_id
  LEFT JOIN results r ON r.assessment_id = a.id AND r.student_id = e.student_id
  GROUP BY e.student_id, e.course_id, c.title, s.name
)
, ranked AS (
  SELECT student_id, name, course, mark,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY student_id ORDER BY mark DESC, course) AS n
  FROM marks
)
SELECT name, COUNT(*) AS courses, ROUND(AVG(mark), 1) AS average,
       MAX(CASE WHEN n = 1 THEN course END) AS best_course
FROM ranked
GROUP BY student_id, name
ORDER BY average DESC, name;

questions.prompt: Why start the marks from enrolments and assessments, not from results?

choices.label: Work not handed in has no result row, and must still count as 0

questions.explanation: Start from what should exist, then LEFT JOIN what does.

questions.prompt: Why does the LEFT JOIN to results match on both assessment and student?

choices.label: So each enrolled student gets only their own result for each assessment

questions.explanation: Matching on the assessment alone would bring in everyone's scores.

questions.prompt: What does `COALESCE(r.score, 0)` do for missing work?

choices.label: Counts it as a score of 0

questions.explanation: A missing hand-in is worth nothing.

questions.prompt: Why multiply whole numbers first and divide by 100.0 at the end?

choices.label: Whole-number sums are exact, so equal marks really tie

questions.explanation: Decimal steps like 0.3 * 88 can leave tiny rounding differences.

questions.prompt: Which aggregate keyword limits COUNT(*) to some rows, as in counting the A grades?
questions.explanation: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE mark >= 80)`.

questions.prompt: Which finds work not handed in?

choices.label: WHERE score IS NULL in results
NOT EXISTS a result for that student and assessment

questions.explanation: There is no row to find a NULL in.

questions.prompt: Two students both have 88.0 on Maths. With RANK, what is the next student's place?
questions.explanation: RANK skips after a tie.

questions.prompt: Why ORDER BY mark DESC, course for the best course?

choices.label: So a tie between two courses always picks the same one

questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER needs an order that doesn't tie.

questions.prompt: Why can't the SELECT list use the alias `last_score` to work out `change`?

choices.label: An alias can't be used elsewhere in the same SELECT list

questions.explanation: Repeat the expression, or use a CTE.

choices.label: How many results that student has on that course, on each of their rows

questions.explanation: A window keeps every row.

intro.title: A library's loans
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A small library wants to know where its books are. The library owns `books`, and of some books it has more than one physical `copies`. `members` borrow copies: each row of `loans` has the copy, the member, the date it was borrowed, the date it is due back (three weeks later) and the date it came back, `returned_on`, which is **NULL while the copy is still out**.

So a loan joins to its book through its copy: `loans → copies → books`. Today is 2026-10-24.

```
SELECT b.title, m.name AS member, l.due_on
FROM loans l
JOIN copies c ON c.id = l.copy_id
JOIN books b ON b.id = c.book_id
JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL
ORDER BY l.due_on, b.title;
```

Dates are text in the form `YYYY-MM-DD`, so comparing them with `<` and `>` works, and `julianday()` turns them into day numbers to subtract. A loan is overdue when it is still out and its due date is before today.

Watch the counts in this capstone: a book with two copies, each with several loans, makes many rows when joined, so count with care, or count in subqueries.

challenges.title: Easy: Overdue
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the loans that are overdue today: `title`, `member` and whole days overdue (`days_overdue`). Most overdue first, then by title.
challenges.hint: Still out and `l.due_on < '2026-10-24'`; `CAST(julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(l.due_on) AS INTEGER)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT b.title, m.name AS member,
       CAST(julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(l.due_on) AS INTEGER) AS days_overdue
FROM loans l
JOIN copies c ON c.id = l.copy_id
JOIN books b ON b.id = c.book_id
JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL AND l.due_on < '2026-10-24'
ORDER BY days_overdue DESC, b.title;

challenges.title: Easy: Loans by genre
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `genre` and its number of `loans`, ever. Most first, then by genre.
challenges.hint: Join loans to copies and books; group by genre.
challenges.solution:
SELECT b.genre, COUNT(*) AS loans
FROM loans l
JOIN copies c ON c.id = l.copy_id
JOIN books b ON b.id = c.book_id
GROUP BY b.genre
ORDER BY loans DESC, b.genre;

challenges.title: Medium: On the shelf
challenges.promptMarkdown: For every book, show `title`, its number of `copies`, how many are out now (`out`) and how many are on the shelf (`available`). Sort by title.
challenges.hint: Count copies and open loans in two subqueries in the SELECT list, so the counts don't multiply each other.
challenges.solution:
SELECT b.title,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM copies c WHERE c.book_id = b.id) AS copies,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans l JOIN copies c ON c.id = l.copy_id
        WHERE c.book_id = b.id AND l.returned_on IS NULL) AS out,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM copies c WHERE c.book_id = b.id)
         - (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans l JOIN copies c ON c.id = l.copy_id
            WHERE c.book_id = b.id AND l.returned_on IS NULL) AS available
FROM books b
ORDER BY b.title;

challenges.title: Medium: Late returns
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the loans that came back late: `member`, `title` and whole days late (`days_late`). Latest first, then by member, then title.
challenges.hint: `WHERE l.returned_on > l.due_on`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT m.name AS member, b.title,
       CAST(julianday(l.returned_on) - julianday(l.due_on) AS INTEGER) AS days_late
FROM loans l
JOIN copies c ON c.id = l.copy_id
JOIN books b ON b.id = c.book_id
JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
WHERE l.returned_on > l.due_on
ORDER BY days_late DESC, member, b.title;

challenges.title: Medium: Fines
challenges.promptMarkdown: The fine is 0.25 for each day late: for loans returned late, up to the day they came back; for overdue loans still out, up to today. Show each member who owes something: `name` and `fine` (2 decimals). Highest first, then by name.
challenges.hint: Days late is `julianday(COALESCE(l.returned_on, '2026-10-24')) - julianday(l.due_on)`; keep loans where it is more than 0.
challenges.solution:
SELECT m.name,
       ROUND(SUM(0.25 * (julianday(COALESCE(l.returned_on, '2026-10-24')) - julianday(l.due_on))), 2) AS fine
FROM loans l
JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
WHERE julianday(COALESCE(l.returned_on, '2026-10-24')) > julianday(l.due_on)
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY fine DESC, m.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Most borrowed in each genre
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each `genre`, show its most borrowed book (`title`, and `loans`). Keep ties. Sort by genre, then title.
challenges.hint: Loans per book in a CTE with `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY b.genre ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC)`; keep 1.
challenges.solution:
WITH counts AS (
  SELECT b.genre, b.title, COUNT(*) AS loans,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY b.genre ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS place
  FROM loans l
  JOIN copies c ON c.id = l.copy_id
  JOIN books b ON b.id = c.book_id
  GROUP BY b.id, b.genre, b.title
)
SELECT genre, title, loans
FROM counts
WHERE place = 1
ORDER BY genre, title;

challenges.title: Hard: How long books stay out
challenges.promptMarkdown: For returned loans, show per `genre`: how many (`returned`), the average days kept (`average_days`, 1 decimal) and the longest (`longest_days`). Sort by genre.
challenges.hint: `julianday(l.returned_on) - julianday(l.borrowed_on)`, only `WHERE l.returned_on IS NOT NULL`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT b.genre, COUNT(*) AS returned,
       ROUND(AVG(julianday(l.returned_on) - julianday(l.borrowed_on)), 1) AS average_days,
       CAST(MAX(julianday(l.returned_on) - julianday(l.borrowed_on)) AS INTEGER) AS longest_days
FROM loans l
JOIN copies c ON c.id = l.copy_id
JOIN books b ON b.id = c.book_id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY b.genre
ORDER BY b.genre;

challenges.title: Expert: Every month
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every month (`month`, like `2026-05`) from the month of the first loan to the month of the last, with the number of loans borrowed in it (`loans`, 0 if none). In order.
challenges.hint: A recursive CTE of month starts: begin at `date(MIN(borrowed_on), 'start of month')`, add `'+1 month'`. LEFT JOIN loans on `strftime('%Y-%m', …)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE months(start) AS (
  SELECT date(MIN(borrowed_on), 'start of month') FROM loans
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(start, '+1 month') FROM months
  WHERE date(start, '+1 month') <= (SELECT MAX(borrowed_on) FROM loans)
)
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', m.start) AS month, COUNT(l.id) AS loans
FROM months m
LEFT JOIN loans l ON strftime('%Y-%m', l.borrowed_on) = strftime('%Y-%m', m.start)
GROUP BY m.start
ORDER BY month;

challenges.title: Expert: Every copy out
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the books with no copy on the shelf right now: `title`, `copies`, and the earliest due date among their open loans (`back_by`). Soonest first, then by title.
challenges.hint: Group open loans by book, and compare their count with the number of copies in HAVING.
challenges.solution:
SELECT b.title, COUNT(*) AS copies, MIN(l.due_on) AS back_by
FROM loans l
JOIN copies c ON c.id = l.copy_id
JOIN books b ON b.id = c.book_id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL
GROUP BY b.id, b.title
HAVING COUNT(*) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM copies c2 WHERE c2.book_id = b.id)
ORDER BY back_by, b.title;

intro.title: Cleaning a messy import
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Real data is rarely tidy. A new app imported its first sign-ups from a web form and a spreadsheet, and `signups` shows it: emails in mixed case with stray spaces, the same person signed up twice, plans written `Basic`, `basic ` and ` PRO`, dates in two formats, phone numbers with brackets and dashes, and empty strings where NULL was meant.

Cleaning goes in a safe order: **look** first (what values are really there?), then **query** the cleaned version without changing anything, and only when that looks right, **change** the data or copy it into a clean table.

```
SELECT plan, COUNT(*) AS signups FROM signups GROUP BY plan ORDER BY plan;
```

The tools are ones you know. `trim()` takes spaces off both ends and `lower()` evens out case, so `lower(trim(email))` is the email to compare by. `NULLIF(trim(x), '')` turns blank text into a real NULL. `replace()` strips characters. `substr()` and `||` rebuild `05/03/2026` (day/month/year) as `2026-03-05`, and `LIKE '__/__/____'` spots that format, since `_` matches any one character.

Duplicates are rows whose cleaned email is the same. Keep the first (lowest id) of each and remove the rest: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY lower(trim(email)) ORDER BY id)` numbers each person's sign-ups, and number 1 is the one to keep.

challenges.title: Expert: A clean table
challenges.promptMarkdown: Create `customers` with `id` (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY), `name` (TEXT NOT NULL), `email` (TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE), `city` (TEXT), `phone` (TEXT), `signed_up` (TEXT NOT NULL), `plan` (TEXT NOT NULL, one of `basic`, `pro`, `team`) and `referred_by` (TEXT). Fill it from signups with one cleaned row per email: keep the lowest id's row and its id, clean every column as in Clean in place, and store phones as digits, with NULL instead of an invalid one.
challenges.hint: CREATE TABLE with `CHECK (plan IN (…))`, then `INSERT INTO customers SELECT …cleaned columns… FROM signups WHERE id IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM signups GROUP BY lower(trim(email)))`. For the phone: `CASE WHEN length(d) = 11 AND d LIKE '07%' THEN d END` on the digits.

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  city TEXT,
  phone TEXT,
  signed_up TEXT NOT NULL,
  plan TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (plan IN ('basic', 'pro', 'team')),
  referred_by TEXT
);

INSERT INTO customers (id, name, email, city, phone, signed_up, plan, referred_by)
SELECT id, trim(full_name), lower(trim(email)),
       upper(substr(trim(city), 1, 1)) || lower(substr(trim(city), 2)),
       CASE WHEN length(replace(replace(replace(replace(phone, ' ', ''), '-', ''), '(', ''), ')', '')) = 11 AND replace(replace(replace(replace(phone, ' ', ''), '-', ''), '(', ''), ')', '') LIKE '07%'
            THEN replace(replace(replace(replace(phone, ' ', ''), '-', ''), '(', ''), ')', '') END,
       CASE WHEN signed_up LIKE '__/__/____'
       THEN substr(signed_up, 7, 4) || '-' || substr(signed_up, 4, 2) || '-' || substr(signed_up, 1, 2)
       ELSE signed_up END,
       lower(trim(plan)),
       NULLIF(trim(referred_by), '')
FROM signups
WHERE id IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM signups GROUP BY lower(trim(email)));

intro.title: Building a booking system
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The last capstone builds a database instead of only reading one. A family runs a few holiday cottages, and until now every booking request has gone into a spreadsheet. Two sheets have been loaded as they are: `cottage_sheet` (each cottage, how many it sleeps and its nightly rate) and `requests` (who asked for which cottage, when, and for how many people).

Over ten steps you'll design proper tables, move the data across, find and fix double bookings, speed up the lookups and build the reports. **Each step starts from the sheets again**, so the starter code carries all your earlier steps; add the new step after them. If an earlier step was wrong, fix it in the starter.

The design: `cottages` and `guests` each get an id, and `bookings` points to both, one row per stay. A stay is from `arrive` to `depart`, and the guests sleep the nights in between: arriving on the 2nd and leaving on the 5th is 3 nights, and someone else can arrive on the 5th.

```
cottages (id, name, sleeps, nightly_rate)
guests   (id, name, email)
bookings (id, guest_id → guests, cottage_id → cottages, arrive, depart, party)
```

Two stays at the same cottage clash when each starts before the other ends: `a.arrive < b.depart AND b.arrive < a.depart`. That one condition covers every kind of overlap, and stays that only touch (one leaves the day the other arrives) don't count.
